name: Australian English
summary: Australian English is non-rhotic, with a distinctive vowel system (raised KIT and DRESS, fronted GOOSE, FACE/GOAT/PRICE/MOUTH with unusual starting points), a partial trap-bath split, t-flapping, dark l, and in casual speech a high rising terminal. Its three traditional accent labels are Broad, General and Cultivated; General is the default for actors and Cultivated is nearly extinct. Round 2 added: grammar (youse, sentence-final 'but', 'eh', heaps/full, adverbs without -ly, 'sweet as', -o/-ie word formation, 'yeah-no'), vocabulary checked in the Australian National Dictionary Centre (ANDC), vowel IPA from the Australian English phonology article (which cites Cox and Fletcher 2017 and Harrington et al.), and regional notes (South Australia, Victoria, WA, Queensland). Evidence still relies on Wikipedia for vowels and some grammar; ANDC, the Macquarie Dictionary and eWAVE (via a feature page) support vocabulary and two grammar items. Primary phonetic works were not opened directly.

grammar.condition: Macquarie Dictionary: second-person plural; first recorded in the 1890s and from Irish English; still non-standard and divisive in speech and writing. Informal, working-class flavour.

Final particle 'but' meaning 'though' ('Yeah it would fit in but'); eWAVE rates it B (neither pervasive nor extremely rare in Australian English); Wikipedia says especially Western Australia and Queensland (Collins and Peters).

grammar.example_dialect: Yeah it would fit in but.

ANDC: arvo (1920s, 'see you Saturday arvo') shows the Australian habit of clipping a word and adding -o; sanger (sandwich), trackie (tracksuit), Aussie and tradie appear in the entries or as -ie examples. Source 7 lists research on hypocoristics.

ANDC's grammar bibliography lists research titled 'Yeah-No He's a Good Kid' (Burridge and Florey 2002) - so it is a studied Australian discourse feature. Meaning/function not summarised in the opened page: LOW confidence. Example constructed.
Source 1: litotes such as 'not bad' for good. Shared with British English; Australian flavour comes from tone.

pronunciation.rule: Non-rhoticity: r is not pronounced after a vowel at the end of a word or before a consonant.
pronunciation.actor_tip: 'car' -> 'cah', 'bird' -> 'buhd'. Keep r before a vowel ('car alarm').

pronunciation.rule: Linking and intrusive r: linking r between words; an r can be inserted where the spelling has none ('drawing' -> 'draw-ring').
pronunciation.actor_tip: Add a soft r when a word ending in a vowel meets a vowel: 'saw it' -> 'saw-r-it'.
pronunciation.example: car alarm, drawing, law and order

pronunciation.rule: PRICE: starts back and rounded-open: General [ɒe]; Cultivated [a̠e]; Broad starts higher and rounder [ɒːe].
pronunciation.actor_tip: Open the mouth, lips slightly rounded at the start, glide up. 'my' like 'moy' for Broad.

pronunciation.rule: MOUTH: General [æo]; Cultivated [a̠ʊ]; Broad [ɛːo] with a fronted, raised start.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Start with 'a' as in cat and glide to 'o'.

pronunciation.rule: FACE: low start, [æ̠ɪ] in General; Cultivated [ɛɪ]; Broad [a̠ːɪ]. GOAT: [æ̠ʉ] in General; Cultivated [ö̞ʊ]; before l the vowel is backed [ɔʊ] (spreading from South Australia).
pronunciation.actor_tip: 'day' with a low start ('dai'); 'go' like 'gaoh' with a fronted second part.

pronunciation.rule: KIT is raised toward [i] (younger speakers now lowering); DRESS [e] raised (Broad even higher); TRAP [æ] (younger often [a]); BAD [æː] long.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Keep 'bit' and 'bet' close and high: 'bet' like 'bait' without glide.

pronunciation.rule: FLEECE and GOOSE: FLEECE [ɪi]-like; GOOSE fronted [ʉː] (ɪ̈ɯ). GOOSE is further forward in NSW than Victoria and moving forward everywhere.
pronunciation.actor_tip: 'see' starts with a short ih; 'too' pushed forward with rounded lips.

pronunciation.rule: START/PALM/BATH: central /ɐː/; the trap-bath split is partial: more words in South Australia ('dance', 'plant'); Tasmania/Victoria prefer the short vowel. Survey: 'graph' /ɐː/ for 86% of Adelaide speakers and /æ/ for 100% of Hobart speakers.
pronunciation.ipa: /ɐː/ in start, palm, bath; /æ/ vs /ɐː/ in dance, graph
pronunciation.actor_tip: 'bath', 'grass' use a central long 'ah'; check 'dance' by state.

pronunciation.rule: Mary-marry-merry: Australian English keeps all three words distinct (no merger).
pronunciation.ipa: no merger (IPA not given in the source)
pronunciation.actor_tip: Say three different vowels; most Americans merge them, Australians do not.

pronunciation.rule: happY tensing: word-final -y in happy/city is a long [iː] (happee).
T-flapping: t (and d) after a stressed vowel and before a weak vowel is a tap [ɾ]; some speakers use a glottal stop for final t.
Dark l in almost all positions; l-vocalisation is more common in South Australia (round-1 item, source 1).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Keep the tongue tip low and the back raised.

pronunciation.rule: Yod-dropping after s, l, z, th: 'suit' = 'soot', 'lute' = 'loot'.
NURSE: [ɜː], as high as [ɘː] and sometimes rounded [ɵː]; NEAR and SQUARE: SQUARE [eː] (higher than RP); in WA and Queensland NEAR is a two-part [ɪə] and SQUARE [ɛə]; elsewhere a long monophthong.
pronunciation.actor_tip: 'bird' with a rounded, high long vowel; 'square' without the 'uh' glide in most states.

intonation.rule: High rising terminal (HRT, 'uptalk'): statements end with a rising pitch and can sound like questions. A 1986 Sydney study (source 1) found it spread among young people from the 1960s, used more by younger than older speakers, and more by women.
intonation.actor_tip: Use on casual statements of fact from young or relaxed speakers; do not use on serious or emotional lines.

intonation.rule: Question-tag and particle melody: 'eh' (Queensland) and sentence-final 'but' are used to check or soften a statement rather than to ask a full question (sources 1, 6). No pitch contour verified.
intonation.actor_tip: Say the statement flat, then let 'eh' / 'but' close the line lightly.

common_mistakes: 'G'day mate', 'crikey', 'strewth' in every speech. Stereotype; use g'day or mate once, if at all.
Applying uptalk to serious or formal lines.
Dropping r at the start of words or before vowels. Only coda r is dropped.
Making every short-a word 'father'. The long vowel is a partial split that varies by state.
Crocodile Dundee 'Strine' exaggeration. Use General Australian by default.
Turning every t between vowels into a full t, losing the flap.
Using 'sheila' for a modern character. Dated and may offend.
Treating 'youse' as neutral; it is non-standard and divisive (Macquarie).
Treating 'no worries' as the only Aussie phrase; use it once.
Forgetting the raised KIT and DRESS vowels; most listeners notice these.
generational_notes: Source 1: Broad is declining in the current generation; Cultivated is nearly extinct. General Australian is the default.
Source 3: KIT is lowering and TRAP moving toward [a] among younger speakers; GOOSE and GOAT are changing (fronting; backed GOAT before l spreading from South Australia).
Source 1: HRT was spread by young people from the 1960s; more by younger than older speakers and by women (1986 Sydney study).
ANDC dates: 'no worries' from the 1960s; 'sanger' from the 1960s; 'dag' (nerd sense) from the 1960s; 'bogan' popularised in the 1980s. Older: g'day (1880s), fair dinkum (1881), sheila (1832).
Younger characters use less g'day/fair dinkum; older ones keep fuller Broad vowels.
conversion_guidelines: Natural spoken film-dialogue English first; add Australian features lightly.
Default General Australian. Use Broad only for rural/working-class older characters; avoid Cultivated unless the text calls for it.
Grammar (one or two per monologue): sentence-final 'but', 'heaps good', 'sweet as', 'eh' tag (Queensland), -o/-ie words. 'Youse' only for plain, working-class characters. 'Yeah-no' is low confidence.
Vocabulary: one or two words (arvo, snag, esky, ute, bludger, no worries) where the text fits. Check age: 'sheila' is dated; 'fair dinkum' is old-fashioned.
Sound notes (to actor): raised KIT/DRESS, General PRICE/MOUTH, t-flap, dark l, non-rhotic with intrusive r.
HRT on casual statements; not on serious lines.
Mark the state (e.g. South Australia) when the speaker is from there.

Hypocoristic rules (-o, -ie) are documented in ANDC bibliography titles; the opened pages did not describe the rules in full.
'Yeah-no' function is from a bibliography title only. 'She'll be right', 'good on you' and 'knowed' were not found in opened sources; omitted.
Intonation beyond HRT is not verified. HRT frequency among current young speakers not checked since the 1986 Sydney study.
Aboriginal English and ethnocultural varieties (Lebanese, Vietnamese, Samoan) are only named; features not verified.
Whether 'eh' is Queensland-specific or national is not clear from source 1.
Age labels for fair dinkum/g'day are coaching judgement; ANDC gives dates, not current frequency.

confidence_detail: medium-high for vocabulary dates/meanings, 'youse' and sentence-final 'but' (ANDC, Macquarie, eWAVE opened); medium for vowels (Wikipedia citing Cox and Fletcher 2017); medium-low for other grammar items and for intonation (one Wikipedia summary of the 1986 study).
